desc:
You start with an array of n zeros. In one operation you choose any contiguous range of positions and add 1 to every element in that range.

Given the array target, return the minimum number of operations needed to turn the zero array into target.

Example: target = [3, 1, 5, 4, 2] returns 7. The target climbs by 3 at the first position (from the imaginary 0 to 3) and by 4 at the third (from 1 to 5); the other steps are flat or falls. That is 3 + 4 = 7 ranges, and fewer cannot create those climbs.
hints: Work out what each operation does to the differences between neighbours, target[i] - target[i-1].
A range operation adds 1 to the difference at its left end and subtracts 1 from the difference just after its right end. Everything else is unchanged.
Every position where the target climbs (target[i] > target[i-1], with an imaginary 0 before the first element) needs at least that many ranges to start there. Sum the climbs.
editorial: Treat target[-1] = 0. Each operation increases the difference at its first position by 1, decreases the difference just after its last position by 1 (if that position exists), and changes no other difference. To create a climb of size d = target[i] - target[i-1] > 0 we need at least d ranges that start at i. Falls never need extra ranges: they are produced by ending ranges that are already open.

So the lower bound is the sum of all positive rises: target[0] + sum(max(0, target[i] - target[i-1])). It is also achievable: whenever the target rises, start exactly that many new ranges; whenever it falls, end that many of the currently open ranges. Thus the lower bound is exact.
One pass over the array, O(n) time and O(1) space. The answer is at most about 5 * 10<sup>8</sup> here, which fits in 32 bits.
